opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core difference comes down to what object you're actually decomposing. Sparse autoencoders decompose the activations: you take the hidden state at some layer and try to explain it as a sparse combination of feature directions. That's been really productive, but it means you're describing what the network is *representing* at a given point, not the mechanisms that *produce* those representations. Parameter decomposition, things like Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition and the stochastic variant we've worked on since, tries to break the weights themselves into components, where each component is meant to be a piece of the network's actual computation, and on any given input only a small number of those components are needed to reproduce the network's behavior.

For unlearning, that distinction matters a lot. If you find an SAE feature for some dangerous capability, it's not obvious what to do with it. You can clamp or ablate the feature at inference time, but the weights that compute it are still there, smeared across the network, and the model may route around your intervention or reconstruct the information downstream. With parameter components, the thing you've identified *is* a chunk of the weights. So in principle you can just subtract it out of the model, and because the decomposition is trained so that components are minimal and faithful, the hope is you remove that mechanism while leaving everything else largely intact. That's a much more surgical, much more permanent intervention than steering at runtime. It's closer to actually editing the program rather than putting a filter on its outputs.

There's also the issue of reconstruction error. SAEs famously don't perfectly reconstruct activations, and when you splice them back in, model performance drops. That "dark matter" might be exactly where some of the behavior you care about lives. Parameter decomposition is set up so the components sum to the original weights, so you're not losing a chunk of the model by construction. You still have approximation issues on the causal-importance side, but the accounting is cleaner.

For monitoring, the appeal is similar. Instead of asking "which features are lit up," you can ask "which mechanisms is the model using right now?" If a component corresponds to, say, a deception-relevant circuit or some capability you're worried about, you can track whether it's causally important on a given forward pass. That's arguably a more meaningful signal than feature activation, because a feature can be represented without being used, whereas a component being important means the computation actually depends on it.

And I'd add a more conceptual point: SAEs tend to give you features that are partly artifacts of the dictionary size and the sparsity penalty, things like feature splitting and absorption, and they don't naturally tell you how features interact across layers. Parameter decomposition gives you the mechanisms directly, including ones that span multiple layers, so you get something closer to a description of the algorithm rather than a catalog of intermediate variables.

I want to be honest that it's earlier-stage. These methods have been harder to scale, more expensive to train, and sensitive to hyperparameters, and we've mostly validated them on toy models and smaller language models so far. But I think the direction is right, because ultimately for unlearning and for oversight, what you care about is the mechanisms, and the parameters are where the mechanisms live.

r001.rationale: It says parameter components are chunks of the weights that produce a behavior and can, in principle, be subtracted to remove the mechanism.

r002.rationale: It proposes monitoring which mechanisms the model uses and their causal importance, rather than merely tracking which features are activated.

r003.rationale: It mentions SAE feature splitting and absorption, but does not explain that deception can use different activation directions across situations, making it hard to identify as one function.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing is that parameter decomposition is operating on a fundamentally different object than sparse autoencoders are. SAEs are decomposing activations. They're asking, at this particular layer, what directions in activation space seem to be the building blocks of what the model is representing right here. And that's useful, but activations are sort of downstream of the thing we actually care about, which is the mechanism. The parameters are where the computation lives. So when you decompose parameters, you're getting something that's much closer to "here is the piece of the network that does this thing," rather than "here is a feature that shows up when this thing is happening."

And that distinction matters a lot for unlearning specifically. If you want to remove a capability, you don't really want to just suppress a feature at one layer, because the model can often route around that, or the feature at that layer was only one part of a mechanism that's spread across many layers. What you actually want is to find the parameter components that implement the capability and ablate those. With something like attribution-based parameter decomposition, you're decomposing the whole network into components that are, in the ideal case, each responsible for some coherent piece of computation. So unlearning becomes something more like surgery on the mechanism itself. You remove the component, and the behavior goes with it, and ideally the rest of the model is left relatively untouched because the decomposition was designed so that components are minimally overlapping in what they do.

For monitoring, I think the story is a bit different but related. One of the frustrations with SAEs is that you train them on some distribution of activations, and then if the model goes off-distribution, or if there's some rare behavior you care about that just didn't show up much in training, the SAE might not have a clean feature for it. The features you get are very much shaped by what was common in the data. With parameter decomposition, you're in principle decomposing everything the network can do, because you're decomposing the parameters, not a sample of activations. The mechanism for some rare behavior still exists in the weights whether or not it fired during your training run. So you have a somewhat better chance of surfacing components that correspond to things the model could do but doesn't do often, which is exactly the kind of thing you'd want to monitor for.

I should be honest that this is still early. The methods we've got right now scale to small models and toy settings, and there are real open problems about how faithful the decompositions are and how you pick the right hyperparameters. SAEs have a few years of engineering behind them at this point, and they work on frontier-scale models. So I don't want to oversell it. But I do think the conceptual advantage is real. If you care about mechanisms, you should probably be decomposing the thing that implements the mechanisms, and that's the parameters.

r001.rationale: The response says parameter decomposition can identify and ablate parameter components that implement a capability, targeting the mechanism directly for unlearning.

r002.rationale: It discusses surfacing rare behaviors from parameter components, but does not propose triggering monitoring based on the network’s use of a function rather than activation along a direction.

r003.rationale: The response does not explain that deception may appear through different activation directions in different situations or why that complicates SAE identification.

astra-6.text:
I think the main advantage is that parameter decomposition gives you something you can intervene on directly in the model’s weights. With a sparse autoencoder, you’re decomposing activations—you’re identifying features in what the model is doing on particular inputs. That can be useful for monitoring, and you can intervene on those features, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you which parameters implement the behavior you want to remove.

If parameter decomposition works well, you could identify a component that contributes to a particular capability and remove or modify that component. That’s an appealing approach to unlearning, because you’re trying to change the mechanism that produces the behavior. The caveat is that we still have to establish that the capability is actually removed, rather than just harder to elicit, and that we haven’t damaged other capabilities in the process.

For monitoring, the potential benefit is a closer connection between what you’re observing and the computation responsible for it. An activation feature might correlate with a behavior; a parameter component could help explain how that behavior is being produced. You’d still need to look at how those components operate on actual inputs, though. I see these as complementary approaches, with parameter decomposition potentially giving us a more direct handle on the underlying mechanisms.

r001.rationale: It says parameter decomposition provides direct access to model weights and could identify and remove or modify a component contributing to the capability, unlike an activation decomposition that may not identify the implementing parameters.

r002.rationale: It describes a closer connection between observed parameter components and computation, but does not propose triggering monitoring based on the network’s use of a function rather than activation along a direction.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss deception or explain that deception may appear along different activation directions in different situations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main advantage is that parameter decomposition gives you something you can intervene on directly in the model’s computation. With a sparse autoencoder, you’re decomposing activations—you’re trying to understand what representations appear when the model processes an input. With parameter decomposition, you’re trying to break the weights themselves into meaningful computational components.

For unlearning, that gives you a potentially useful target. If you can identify components responsible for a particular capability or piece of knowledge, you could remove or modify those components. With an SAE, suppressing a feature doesn’t necessarily remove the underlying mechanism that produces it. The information might still be available through another representation. Of course, parameter decomposition doesn’t automatically solve that either; you still have to establish that you’ve found all the relevant components and that removing them doesn’t damage other capabilities.

For monitoring, the attraction is that you could potentially track which computational components are contributing to a particular output, rather than just detecting that some concept is represented in the activations. A model representing deception, for example, is different from a model actually using a mechanism to deceive. Ideally, we’d like our monitoring to distinguish those things.

So I’d frame the advantage as getting closer to the mechanisms that generate behavior. Whether we can decompose those mechanisms cleanly enough to make unlearning and monitoring reliable is still an open research question.

r001.rationale: The response says parameter decomposition works on the weights themselves and could identify and modify components responsible for a capability or knowledge.

r002.rationale: It proposes monitoring which computational components contribute to an output, distinguishing a model using a mechanism from merely representing a concept.

r003.rationale: It does not say that deception may appear in different activation directions across situations or that this makes it hard for sparse autoencoders to identify as one functionality.
